prompt.context: Your client is a PE firm that is considering an investment in Dr. Kelso's ophthalmology practice, located outside Philadelphia. Dr. Kelso's practice provides a full range of ophthalmology services including exams, surgeries, and prescribing and administering pharmaceuticals. The practice accepts major commercial and government insurance. Today, Dr. Kelso and 3 other doctor partners are equity owners in the business and are only paid their share of the profits — they do not take a salary. The practice is requesting $15M for a 50% stake in the business. The PE firm's objective is to make a good ROI on the investment.
prompt.question: Should the PE firm make the investment in Dr. Kelso's ophthalmology practice?

clarifying_info.q: How does Dr. Kelso's business make money? What is ophthalmology?
clarifying_info.a: An ophthalmologist is an eye doctor. The practice provides a full range of ophthalmology services including exams, surgeries, and prescribing and administering pharmaceuticals. It accepts major commercial and government insurance.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current ownership structure?
clarifying_info.a: Dr. Kelso and 3 other doctor partners are equity owners. They are only paid their share of the profits and do not take a salary.

clarifying_info.q: What are the terms of the deal?
clarifying_info.a: Dr. Kelso's practice is requesting $15M for a 50% stake in the business.

clarifying_info.q: What are the PE firm's objectives?
clarifying_info.a: To make a good ROI on the investment.

exhibits.title: Financial Forecast
exhibits.shows: A table showing the PE firm's financial projection for Dr. Kelso's practice for next year (2022F), including Revenue, Costs, Operating Profit, Taxes (20%), and Net Profit. Also includes assumptions: WACC = 13%, Growth Rate = 3%. Note states the practice has no depreciation, debt, or investment in CapEx. The Taxes and Net Profit rows are intentionally left blank for the candidate to calculate.

framework: 1. Market: A) Market size (number of customers, insurance vs. cash, market growth, demand); B) Competitors (number, hospital-owned vs. independent, full-suite vs. focused, referral affiliations); C) Trends (teleconsultation, growth of cosmetic surgeries like LASIK)

2. Financials: A) Revenue (price: avg service fee, collections rate, insurance vs. cash; volume: number of patients, insurance vs. cash mix, service mix); B) Costs (variable: labor, materials, marketing; fixed: rent, loans, equipment, utilities)

3. Opportunities: A) Revenue synergies (increase reimbursement via greater market power, increase volume via combination with referrers, increase collection rate via better business management); B) Cost synergies (decrease practice management costs through scale with other portfolio assets)
4. Deal Terms: A) ROI / Payback Period / NPV; B) Ownership structure (is PE stake >50%?); C) Why are the doctors selling?; D) Risks; E) Other opportunities

questions.prompt: The PE firm prepared a financial projection for Dr. Kelso's practice for next year before the deal takes place. Using Exhibit 1, what is the implied valuation of the company today?
questions.guidance: Candidate should complete the income statement, then apply a Gordon Growth Model (perpetuity growth) to derive enterprise value, and finally assess whether the $15M purchase price for 50% is attractive. Strong candidates note that FCF = Net Profit here because there is no depreciation, debt, or CapEx.

math.setup: Complete the income statement: Operating Profit = $20M - $16M = $4M; Taxes = 20% x $4M = $0.8M; Net Profit (= FCF) = $4M - $0.8M = $3.2M. Then apply Gordon Growth Model: Value = FCF / (WACC - g)
steps: ROI = $16M / $15M investment ≈ 7% — not a good return
math.answer: Implied enterprise value = $32M; PE stake worth $16M; ROI ≈ 7% (poor)

questions.prompt: If the PE firm acquired a stake in Dr. Kelso's practice, how could they increase the value of the company?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm both revenue drivers and cost drivers, as well as potential synergies. See brainstorming section for expected structure.

questions.prompt: After initial research the PE firm believes they can improve revenue by 5% via improved pricing and collections, and reduce practice management costs by $1M through cost synergies. What would the PE client's stake be worth with these changes?
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply the improvements to the baseline financials and re-run the valuation. Outstanding candidates will also note the volume-decline breakeven scenario.

math.setup: Apply revenue uplift and cost reduction, recalculate net profit, then re-apply Gordon Growth Model.
steps: Bonus: If volume declines ~10% (revenue falls from $21M to $19M), valuation drops to ~$36M and PE barely breaks even
math.answer: PE stake worth $24M; ROI = 60%. Breakeven if revenue declines ~10% to $19M (valuation ~$36M).

questions.prompt: How would compensation for Dr. Kelso and his 3 partners change after the deal? How do you think this would impact volume?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare pre-deal and post-deal compensation, then reason about incentive effects on physician effort and patient volume.

math.setup: Compare pre-deal profit share with post-deal structure.
steps: Pre-deal: Partners receive 100% of net profit = $3.2M per year
Post-deal (with improvements): Partners receive $24M upfront payout + 50% of $4.8M net profit = $2.4M per year
As 50% equity owners, doctors receive only 50 cents on the dollar for incremental effort — incentive to work hard is reduced
After a $24M windfall payout, doctors have even less financial urgency to maintain volume
math.answer: Partner annual compensation drops from $3.2M (100% of profit) to $2.4M (50% of improved profit). Reduced ownership stake and large upfront payout both reduce motivation, which is expected to decrease patient volume.

questions.prompt: How can the deal be changed to make sure we keep current volume growth at 3%?
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose deal structure modifications that preserve physician incentives.

questions.prompt: The client determines they need to pay $0.6M in performance-based compensation to Dr. Kelso and his partners to keep them sufficiently incentivized and maintain volume growth. With this change, what would the value of the PE firm's stake be?
questions.guidance: Candidate should treat the $0.6M incentive compensation as an additional cost, recalculate net profit, and re-run the valuation.

math.setup: Add $0.6M compensation cost to the improved cost base and recalculate.
steps: Operating Profit = $21M revenue - $15M costs - $0.6M incentive comp = $5.4M
math.answer: PE stake worth ~$21.5M; ROI ≈ 43% — still a good investment.

brainstorming.prompt: If the PE firm acquired a stake in Dr. Kelso's practice, how could they increase the value of the company?

categories.name: Revenue — Pricing & Collections
ideas: Negotiate higher reimbursement rates with insurers via greater market power (e.g., by combining with other portfolio practices)
Improve collections rate through better billing and revenue cycle management
Shift mix toward higher-margin cash-pay services (e.g., LASIK, cosmetic procedures)

categories.name: Revenue — Volume
ideas: Increase patient volume by acquiring or partnering with referral sources (PCPs, optometrists)
Expand service offerings to capture more of the patient's care journey
Add new physicians or extend clinic hours to serve more patients
Leverage teleconsultation to reach patients outside the immediate geography

categories.name: Cost Synergies
ideas: Reduce practice management overhead by sharing administrative/back-office functions across portfolio practices
Consolidate purchasing of medical supplies and equipment for volume discounts
Standardize EHR and billing systems to reduce IT costs

categories.name: Strategic / Deal Structure
ideas: Acquire majority stake (>50%) to gain full operational control
Roll up additional practices in the region to build scale
Explore add-on acquisitions of optometry practices to capture referral volume

recommendation: The PE firm should make the investment in Dr. Kelso's ophthalmology practice — but only if deal-structure safeguards are in place. With a 5% revenue improvement and $1M cost reduction, the ROI rises to 60% ($24M stake value vs. $15M investment). Even after adding $0.6M in performance-based compensation to preserve physician incentives, ROI remains approximately 43% — well above the hurdle rate.
The base-case valuation (no improvements) yields only ~7% ROI, so the investment thesis depends entirely on the PE firm's ability to execute operational improvements.
risks: Doctors lose financial incentive once they receive the $24M upfront payout and hold only a 50% profit share, which could cause volume to decline and erode value
If revenue declines ~10% (from $21M to ~$19M), the PE firm barely breaks even on its investment
Regulatory risk: healthcare reimbursement rates from government and commercial payers can change, compressing margins
Competition from hospital-owned systems or larger ophthalmology groups that have more pricing power with insurers
next_steps: Design and negotiate an effective incentive compensation structure (e.g., performance bonuses, multi-year vesting of deal proceeds tied to volume targets) to align physician behavior with value creation
Conduct commercial due diligence on the local market — number of competitors, referral network strength, and growth potential
Validate the $1M cost synergy assumption by auditing current practice management costs and benchmarking against comparable practices in the PE portfolio
Explore whether a majority stake (>50%) is achievable to gain full operational control
